641.event_title: Cicero, a 'new man', wins the consulship through his oratory
641.event: Marcus Tullius Cicero came from a wealthy equestrian family with no consuls among his ancestors, and he built his career largely on his work as an advocate in the law courts, including his successful prosecution of Verres in 70 BCE. He rose through each office at the minimum legal age and was elected consul for 63 BCE as a novus homo, a 'new man', heading the poll. He is remembered as the greatest Roman orator, and his speeches against Catiline during his consulship are among his best-known works.
641.explanation: Without noble birth or a military record, Cicero reached the highest office of the Republic mainly through the power of his speech.
641.tie_back: The kural calls the goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right, not merely one good among others, and Cicero's rise shows eloquence serving as the capital that a lack of lineage denied him.
641._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of eloquence as a possession in its own right; other factors, including political alliances, also helped Cicero's election.

642.event_title: A loosely worded order sends the Light Brigade down the wrong valley
642.event: During the Battle of Balaklava in the Crimean War, Lord Raglan sent a written order for the cavalry to advance rapidly to the front and try to prevent the enemy carrying away the guns. The cavalry commanders could not see which guns he meant from their position, and the Light Brigade charged instead at a Russian battery at the end of a heavily defended valley. Of the roughly 670 men who charged, about 260 were killed or wounded, and the episode became one of the most infamous blunders in British military history.
642.explanation: The order made perfect sense from Raglan's viewpoint on the heights but was dangerously ambiguous to those who had to carry it out, and no one stopped to clarify it.
642.tie_back: The kural warns that both prosperity and ruin come through words, so one must guard against any lapse in speech, and the vague wording of a single order at Balaklava turned into disaster.
642._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of ruin flowing from a lapse in wording, though the misunderstanding also involved the way the order was relayed and the commanders' failure to ask for clarification.

643.event_title: Swami Vivekananda addresses the World's Parliament of Religions
643.event: On the opening day of the World's Parliament of Religions, held during the Chicago World's Fair, the Hindu monk Swami Vivekananda began his address by greeting the audience as sisters and brothers of America. The crowd of thousands rose and gave him a long ovation, and his short speech on tolerance and the rejection of fanaticism made him one of the stars of the Parliament. Afterwards he lectured widely across the United States on Hindu philosophy and founded the Vedanta Society in New York.
643.explanation: An unknown delegate from India won over a large foreign audience in a few minutes, and the demand to hear him again carried him on lecture tours for years.
643.tie_back: The kural describes true eloquence as speech that binds those who hear it and makes even those who have not heard it long to hear it, which is what Vivekananda's Chicago address did.
643._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a speech that captivated its hearers and created a wider wish to hear the speaker.

644.event_title: John F. Kennedy speaks to West Berliners in their own words
644.place: Rudolph Wilde Platz, West Berlin, West Germany
644.event: Two years after the Berlin Wall went up, President John F. Kennedy spoke to a vast crowd of West Berliners outside the Rathaus Schoeneberg. Early in the speech he declared Ich bin ein Berliner, a German phrase he had practised beforehand with his interpreter Robert Lochner in Mayor Willy Brandt's office, to show that the United States stood with the people of the divided city. The line bonded him to his audience and became one of the best-known moments of the Cold War.
644.explanation: Kennedy's message was not new, but he shaped it to the exact fears, pride and language of the people in front of him.
644.tie_back: The kural says to speak only after understanding the nature of one's hearers, since nothing is worth more than speech fitted to them, and Kennedy's Berlin speech is a celebrated example of exactly that.
644._accuracy_note: A very close fit: the speech's power came from tailoring words to a specific audience.

645.event_title: Gandhi pleads guilty at the Great Trial in Ahmedabad
645.event: Charged with sedition for three articles in his weekly Young India, Mohandas Gandhi pleaded guilty before Judge Robert Broomfield, leaving the prosecution nothing to prove. He then read a written statement explaining how he had turned from loyalty to the British Empire to non-cooperation, and said he was there to submit to the highest penalty the law could impose for what he regarded as the highest duty of a citizen. The judge, acknowledging that many regarded Gandhi as a great patriot, sentenced him to six years and said no one would be better pleased than he if the government later reduced the sentence.
645.explanation: By admitting the facts and accepting the penalty in advance, Gandhi left no ground for argument against him and turned the trial into an examination of British rule.
645.tie_back: The kural advises speaking only after making sure no other word can defeat one's own, and Gandhi's carefully prepared statement left the court with nothing to refute.
645._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Gandhi's words were unanswerable in argument, though he still received the sentence.

646.event_title: Mahalia Jackson's call and King's dream
646.place: Lincoln Memorial, Washington, D.C., United States
646.event: Martin Luther King Jr. was the final official speaker at the March on Washington, before a crowd of some 250,000 people, and he began by reading his prepared text. As he neared the end, the singer Mahalia Jackson called out to him to tell the crowd about the dream, a theme he had used at earlier events. King turned aside from his manuscript and spoke extemporaneously about his dream, and these improvised passages became the most celebrated part of the speech.
646.explanation: King was able both to hold a huge audience and to take in a single call from a friend nearby, seize its value and use it at once.
646.tie_back: The kural praises those who speak so that others long to hear and who also grasp the useful meaning of what others say, and King's response to Jackson's call shows both skills in one moment.
646._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of speaking and listening together, with the caveat that King himself described the shift as a response to the crowd and did not say whether he heard Jackson.

647.event_title: Nelson Mandela's statement from the dock at the Rivonia Trial
647.event: Facing charges of sabotage that could carry the death penalty, Nelson Mandela opened the defence case at the Rivonia Trial by making a statement from the dock instead of giving evidence under cross-examination. In a long statement he explained his actions and the cause of a free and democratic society, ending with the declaration that it was an ideal for which he was prepared to die. On 12 June 1964 Judge Quartus de Wet sentenced him and seven others to life imprisonment, saying he had decided not to impose the supreme penalty.
647.explanation: Mandela spoke without fear, without faltering and with great force in a hostile courtroom, and his statement became one of the most famous speeches of the twentieth century.
647.tie_back: The kural says no one can easily overcome a speaker who is powerful, never slips and does not fear, and Mandela's statement from the dock was not defeated even though he lost the case.
647._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Mandela showed every quality the kural names, but he was still convicted, so the 'victory' lies in the speech's lasting force rather than in the verdict.

648.event_title: Roosevelt's first fireside chat ends the bank panic
648.event: After declaring a nationwide bank holiday, President Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke to Americans by radio on 12 March 1933, explaining in plain, orderly terms what had happened to the banks, how the new Emergency Banking Act would work, and when sound banks would reopen. When banks reopened the next day, long lines of customers came to return their hoarded cash, and by the end of March the public had redeposited about two-thirds of the currency withdrawn in the panic. On 15 March the New York Stock Exchange recorded its largest one-day percentage gain.
648.explanation: The broadcast worked because Roosevelt laid out the situation step by step in a warm, direct manner, and millions of listeners acted on what he asked of them within days.
648.tie_back: The kural says that if the world finds someone who can speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do what that person asks, and the public's swift return to the banks after Roosevelt's talk is a clear case.
648._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, though the new law and federal backing of the banks also contributed to the restored confidence.

649.event_title: Lincoln's two-minute Gettysburg Address follows a two-hour oration
649.event: At the dedication of the national cemetery at Gettysburg, the main address was a two-hour oration of some 13,000 words by Edward Everett, the best-known orator of the day. President Abraham Lincoln then spoke for barely more than two minutes, delivering 272 words. The next day Everett wrote to Lincoln that he wished he had come as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
649.explanation: Lincoln's brief, carefully chosen words became one of the most celebrated speeches in history, while the far longer oration is now largely forgotten.
649.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot say a few flawless words are the ones who love to say many, and the contrast at Gettysburg, acknowledged by Everett himself, shows the power of a few faultless words.
649._accuracy_note: A very close fit for the value of few faultless words, though Everett was a skilled orator rather than an unskilled talker, so only the positive half of the kural is shown.

650.event_title: Fukuzawa Yukichi publishes An Encouragement of Learning in plain Japanese
650.event: After travelling to the United States and Europe in the 1860s, Fukuzawa Yukichi published Seiyo jijo (Conditions in the West) and then, between 1872 and 1876, the seventeen essays of Gakumon no susume (An Encouragement of Learning). He condensed ideas from Western books into a message of his own and wrote as plainly as possible so that young readers could follow it, and the work was even used as an elementary school textbook. By his own estimate the first essay alone sold about 220,000 copies, many of them pirated, at a time when Japan had about 35 million people.
650.explanation: Fukuzawa's learning mattered to Meiji Japan because he could unfold it in clear, simple language that ordinary readers understood.
650.tie_back: The kural compares learned people who cannot explain what they know to flowers that bloom without fragrance, and Fukuzawa is the opposite case, a scholar whose learning spread its fragrance because he explained it so clearly.
650._accuracy_note: A strong illustration in positive form of what the kural recommends, rather than an example of the scentless flower it warns against.
